title: What security features have you implemented, and explain a JWT + OAuth2 implementation end-to-end (JwtUtil, filter, security config, login endpoint)?
shortTitle: What security features have you implemented, and explain a JWT + OAuth2 implementation end-to-end

s1_definition.profdef: A JWT plus OAuth2 implementation in Spring Security is a stateless authentication scheme where a login endpoint verifies credentials and a `JwtUtil` mints a signed JSON Web Token, a once-per-request authentication filter extracts and validates that token on every subsequent call and populates the security context, and a security configuration class defines which endpoints are public, which require authentication, and wires the filter into the chain. OAuth2 provides the overall authorization framework and token-issuance model, while the JWT is the self-contained signed access token the services trust without a central session store.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India gives each customer a tamper-proof wristband when they prove their identity at the entrance, that is the login endpoint minting a JWT. For the rest of their visit, every department simply scans the wristband to confirm it is genuine and not expired, instead of phoning the entrance desk again, that is the filter validating the token on every request. The bank's rulebook says which areas are open to all and which need a scanned wristband, that is the security configuration. Because the wristband itself proves who you are and what you can do, no department needs to keep a running list of who is currently inside, which is what stateless means.
s1_definition.oneliner: The login endpoint verifies credentials and JwtUtil signs a token, a once-per-request filter validates it and sets the security context, and the security config declares which routes are public versus protected and plugs the filter in, giving stateless OAuth2-style authentication.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A JWT plus OAuth2 implementation in Spring Security is a stateless authentication scheme where a login endpoint verifies credentials and a `JwtUtil` mints a signed JSON Web Token, a once-per-request authentication filter extracts and validates that token on every subsequent call and populates the security context, and a security configuration class defines which endpoints are public, which require authentication, and wires the filter into the chain. OAuth2 provides the overall authorization framework and token-issuance model, while the JWT is the self-contained signed access token the services trust without a central session store.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India gives each customer a tamper-proof wristband when they prove their identity at the entrance, that is the login endpoint minting a JWT. For the rest of their visit, every department simply scans the wristband to confirm it is genuine and not expired, instead of phoning the entrance desk again, that is the filter validating the token on every request. The bank's rulebook says which areas are open to all and which need a scanned wristband, that is the security configuration. Because the wristband itself proves who you are and what you can do, no department needs to keep a running list of who is currently inside, which is what stateless means.

**One line to remember:** The login endpoint verifies credentials and JwtUtil signs a token, a once-per-request filter validates it and sets the security context, and the security config declares which routes are public versus protected and plugs the filter in, giving stateless OAuth2-style authentication.

sections.s2_technical:
Begin with the overall security features typically implemented in a banking platform, so the end-to-end flow has context. These include stateless JWT authentication, role-based authorization with method and URL rules, password hashing with BCrypt so raw passwords are never stored, HTTPS everywhere, CORS configured to allow only trusted origins, CSRF protection disabled for stateless token APIs because there is no cookie session to forge, protection against common injection through parameterized queries and validation, short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, and centralized exception handling that returns clean 401 and 403 responses without leaking internals. The JWT plus OAuth2 piece is the authentication backbone those features build on.

The `JwtUtil` is the component that creates and verifies tokens. On creation it builds the claims, typically the subject which is the username, the roles or authorities, an issued-at timestamp, and an expiry, then signs the whole thing with a secret key for HMAC or a private key for RSA, producing the compact token string. For example a method `generateToken(username, roles)` sets the subject, puts the roles in a claim, sets expiry to the current time plus a configured duration, and signs it. For verification it parses the token with the same key, which fails if the signature is invalid or the token is expired, and exposes helpers like `extractUsername(token)` and `isTokenValid(token, userDetails)`. Keeping all token logic in one utility means the filter and the login endpoint share exactly one implementation.

The authentication filter is where validation happens on every request. It extends `OncePerRequestFilter` so it runs exactly once per request, reads the `Authorization` header, checks it starts with `Bearer `, extracts the token, and uses `JwtUtil` to validate it and read the username. If the token is valid and no authentication is already set, it loads the user's authorities, builds a `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken`, and places it into the `SecurityContextHolder`. From that point Spring treats the request as authenticated with the right roles, and downstream authorization annotations work. If the token is missing or invalid, the filter simply does not set authentication, and the security chain later rejects protected endpoints with a 401.

The security configuration class wires everything together. In modern Spring Security you define a `SecurityFilterChain` bean where you set the session policy to stateless because JWTs carry the state, declare which endpoints are public such as the login and token endpoints, require authentication for everything else, optionally add fine-grained role rules, disable CSRF for the stateless API, and register the JWT filter before the standard username-password filter so it runs first. You also expose a `PasswordEncoder` bean using BCrypt and an `AuthenticationManager` bean used by the login endpoint.

The login endpoint is the entry point that issues tokens. It receives a username and password, delegates to the `AuthenticationManager` to verify them against the stored BCrypt-hashed credentials, and on success calls `JwtUtil.generateToken` to mint the access token, returning it to the client. The client then stores the token and sends it as a bearer header on every subsequent call, which the filter validates. In a full OAuth2 setup the token issuance is delegated to an authorization server and the services act as resource servers validating tokens, but the hand-rolled JwtUtil-and-filter version shown here demonstrates the same mechanics explicitly.

Senior nuances: keep access tokens short-lived and pair them with refresh tokens so a stolen token has a small blast radius; validate the token's issuer and audience, not only its signature; never put sensitive data in the payload because it is only encoded, not encrypted; store the signing key in a secrets manager and rotate it; and return consistent 401 for unauthenticated and 403 for unauthorized so clients and logs are unambiguous.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's API must let Rajesh log in once and then call many protected endpoints without logging in again, and without the services keeping server-side sessions that would not scale across instances. This is exactly the stateless JWT case, where the login endpoint mints a token the services trust on every request.

Problem 2 — Every protected request must be checked automatically, not endpoint by endpoint, so no developer can forget. This is exactly the once-per-request filter, which validates the token centrally and sets the security context.

Problem 3 — Some endpoints, like login itself and a health check, must be public, while account and transfer endpoints must require authentication and the right role. This is exactly the security configuration, which declares public versus protected routes and wires in the filter.

Our mini-project demonstrates the full flow in a runnable way. The code defines a `JwtUtil` that signs and verifies tokens, a `JwtAuthFilter` that validates the bearer token and sets a simple security context, a `SecurityConfig` that lists public and protected paths, a `LoginController` that verifies credentials and returns a token, and a demo that logs Rajesh in, calls a protected endpoint with the token successfully, and shows a missing or invalid token being rejected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's username and password, and a protected account endpoint he wants to reach.

Step 1: Rajesh posts his username and password to the login endpoint. The endpoint verifies the credentials, which in a real system means comparing against the BCrypt-hashed password through the authentication manager. On success it asks `JwtUtil` to mint a token carrying his username, his CUSTOMER role, and an expiry, signed with the secret key.

Step 2: Rajesh receives the token and stores it. From now on he attaches it as an Authorization bearer header on every request, so he never logs in again until it expires.

Step 3: Rajesh calls the protected account endpoint. The once-per-request filter runs first. It sees the path is not public, reads the bearer header, extracts the token, and asks `JwtUtil` to validate the signature and expiry. Both pass, so the filter extracts the username and roles and sets the security context to authenticated.

Step 4: Because the security context now holds an authenticated user with the CUSTOMER role, the account controller runs and returns the account. Authorization annotations, if present, would also see the role and allow the call.

Step 5: Rajesh then makes the same call without a token. The filter finds no bearer header, sets no authentication, and the security configuration rejects the protected endpoint with a 401. Meanwhile the login endpoint remains public, so it needs no token at all. The output shows the token being issued, the authenticated access, and the unauthenticated rejection.

```
2026-10-24 14:52:40 INFO    login issued token (truncated): rajesh|CUSTO...
2026-10-24 14:52:40 INFO    rajesh (roles [CUSTOMER]) viewed account SAV2001
2026-10-24 14:52:40 SEVERE  401 Unauthorized: missing/invalid token
2026-10-24 14:52:40 INFO    /api/auth/login is public? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  POST /api/auth/login {username, password}
    │
    ▼
  LoginController ─ verify via AuthenticationManager (BCrypt)
    │ success
    ▼
  JwtUtil.generateToken(username, roles) ─ sign(secret) ─▶ JWT
    │ returned to client
    ▼
  Client stores token, sends "Authorization: Bearer <JWT>" on every call
    │
    ▼
  GET /api/accounts/SAV2001  (Authorization: Bearer <JWT>)
    │
    ▼
  JwtAuthFilter (OncePerRequestFilter)
    │ public path?         → permit (no token)
    │ Bearer present?      → extract token
    │ JwtUtil.isTokenValid → signature + expiry
    │   valid   → set SecurityContext(user, roles)
    │   invalid → no auth → 401
    ▼
  SecurityConfig: permitAll(public), authenticated(rest), filter before UsernamePwd
    │
    ▼
  AccountController.getAccount  → 200 OK
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
On my banking platform I implemented a set of security features with JWT plus OAuth2 as the authentication backbone: stateless JWT authentication, role-based authorization at the URL and method level, BCrypt password hashing so raw passwords are never stored, HTTPS everywhere, CORS restricted to trusted origins, CSRF disabled for the stateless token API because there is no cookie session to forge, short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, and centralized exception handling that returns clean 401 and 403 responses. The core of it is four pieces: a JwtUtil, an authentication filter, a security configuration, and a login endpoint.

The JwtUtil owns all token logic so there is exactly one implementation. On creation it builds the claims, the subject which is the username, the roles, an issued-at and an expiry, and signs the whole token with the secret key, returning the compact string. For verification it parses with the same key, which fails on a bad signature or an expired token, and it exposes helpers to extract the username and roles and to check validity. Keeping this in one utility means the login endpoint and the filter share the same code.

The authentication filter extends OncePerRequestFilter so it runs exactly once per request. It reads the Authorization header, checks for the Bearer prefix, extracts the token, and uses JwtUtil to validate it and read the username and roles. If valid, it builds an authentication token and places it in the SecurityContextHolder, so from that point Spring treats the request as authenticated with the right roles and authorization annotations work. If the token is missing or invalid, it simply sets no authentication and the chain later rejects protected endpoints with a 401. The security configuration ties it together in a SecurityFilterChain bean: it sets the session policy to stateless because the JWT carries the state, permits the public endpoints like login and health, requires authentication for everything else, disables CSRF for the stateless API, and registers the JWT filter before the standard username-password filter. It also exposes a BCrypt PasswordEncoder and an AuthenticationManager. The login endpoint verifies the username and password through the authentication manager against the stored BCrypt hash and, on success, calls JwtUtil to mint the token and returns it.

On my project at National Bank of India this let Rajesh log in once and then call the account and transfer endpoints with a bearer token the services trusted on every request, with no server-side session, so it scaled across instances cleanly. The filter made validation automatic so no developer could forget it, and the config cleanly separated public routes like login from protected routes like accounts. The nuances I always add are to keep access tokens short-lived with refresh-token rotation so a stolen token has a small blast radius, to validate the token's issuer and audience and not just its signature, to never put sensitive data in the payload because it is only encoded and not encrypted, and to store the signing key in a secrets manager and rotate it.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that the login endpoint verifies credentials and JwtUtil signs a short-lived token, a once-per-request filter validates it and populates the security context, and the security config declares public versus protected routes and wires the filter into a stateless chain, which together give clean, scalable OAuth2-style authentication.
